claim: The position of the mitotic spindle determines the plane of cell cleavage, and thereby daughter cell location, size, and content.
source: The position of the mitotic spindle determines the plane of cell cleavage, and thereby daughter cell location, size, and content.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about spindle positioning and cell division.

claim: Spindle positioning is driven by dynein-mediated pulling forces exerted on astral microtubules.
source: Spindle positioning is driven by dynein-mediated pulling forces exerted on astral microtubules, which requires an evolutionarily conserved complex of Gα∙GDP, GPR-1/2Pins/LGN, and LIN-5Mud/NuMA proteins.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Spindle positioning requires an evolutionarily conserved complex of Gα∙GDP, GPR-1/2Pins/LGN, and LIN-5Mud/NuMA proteins.
source: Spindle positioning is driven by dynein-mediated pulling forces exerted on astral microtubules, which requires an evolutionarily conserved complex of Gα∙GDP, GPR-1/2Pins/LGN, and LIN-5Mud/NuMA proteins.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Gα∙GDP, Gα∙GTP, and GPR-1/2 are not required for pulling-force generation.
source: By replacing Gα and GPR-1/2 with a light-inducible membrane anchor, we demonstrate that Gα∙GDP, Gα∙GTP, and GPR-1/2 are not required for pulling-force generation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Cortical recruitment of LIN-5, but not dynein itself, induced high pulling forces in the absence of Gα and GPR-1/2.
source: In the absence of Gα and GPR-1/2, cortical recruitment of LIN-5, but not dynein itself, induced high pulling forces.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from optogenetic recruitment experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Light-controlled localization of LIN-5 overruled normal cell-cycle and polarity regulation.
source: The light-controlled localization of LIN-5 overruled normal cell-cycle and polarity regulation and provided experimental control over the spindle and cell-cleavage plane.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8 and associated videos.

claim: Light-controlled localization of LIN-5 provided experimental control over the spindle and cell-cleavage plane.
source: The light-controlled localization of LIN-5 overruled normal cell-cycle and polarity regulation and provided experimental control over the spindle and cell-cleavage plane.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8 and associated videos.

claim: Gα∙GDP–GPR-1/2Pins/LGN functions as a regulatable membrane anchor.
source: Our results define Gα∙GDP–GPR-1/2Pins/LGN as a regulatable membrane anchor, and LIN-5Mud/NuMA as a potent activator of dynein-dependent spindle-positioning forces.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing that these components can be replaced by a membrane anchor.

claim: LIN-5Mud/NuMA is a potent activator of dynein-dependent spindle-positioning forces.
source: Our results define Gα∙GDP–GPR-1/2Pins/LGN as a regulatable membrane anchor, and LIN-5Mud/NuMA as a potent activator of dynein-dependent spindle-positioning forces.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that LIN-5 recruitment generates strong pulling forces.

claim: Early work in C. elegans demonstrated that cortical pulling forces position the spindle through a protein complex consisting of Gα, GPR-1/2, and LIN-5.
source: Early work in C. elegans demonstrated that cortical pulling forces position the spindle through a protein complex that consists of a heterotrimeric G protein alpha subunit, GOA-1Gαo or GPA-16Gαi (together referred to as Gα), a TPR-GoLoco domain protein GPR-1/2, and the coiled-coil protein LIN-5 (Colombo et al., 2003; Gotta and Ahringer, 2001; Gotta et al., 2003; Grill et al., 2001; Lorson et al., 2000; Miller and Rand, 2000; Srinivasan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The Gα–GPR-1/2–LIN-5 complex and related complexes in Drosophila and mammals recruit dynein to the cell cortex.
source: This complex, and the closely related Drosophila Gαi/o–Pins–Mud and mammalian Gαi/o–LGN–NuMA protein complexes, recruit the microtubule motor dynein to the cell cortex (Bellaïche et al., 2001; Bowman et al., 2006; Du and Macara, 2004; Du et al., 2001; Izumi et al., 2004; Nguyen-Ngoc et al., 2007; Schaefer et al., 2001; Zheng et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2011) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Processive movement of mammalian cytoplasmic dynein during cargo transport requires a dynein adaptor.
source: Such an adaptor is necessary for the processive movement of mammalian cytoplasmic dynein during cargo transport along microtubules (Reck-Peterson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Reck-Peterson et al., 2018.

claim: Surface-anchored yeast dynein in contact with depolymerizing microtubules generates pulling forces in vitro without an adaptor.
source: Without adaptor, surface-anchored yeast dynein in contact with depolymerizing microtubules generates pulling forces in vitro (Laan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Laan et al., 2012.

claim: Yeast dynein moves processively on its own.
source: However, yeast dynein moves processively on its own (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Reck-Peterson et al., 2006.

claim: It remains unknown whether cortical pulling force generation in animal cells depends just on anchoring of dynein or requires an additional dynein activator.
source: Hence, it remains unknown whether cortical pulling force generation in animal cells depends just on anchoring of dynein, or whether this requires an additional dynein activator.
evidence: This is a statement of the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Membrane-attached Gα∙GDP associates with GoLoco motifs present in GPR-1/2, Pins, and LGN proteins.
source: Membrane-attached Gα∙GDP associates with GoLoco motifs present in the homologous GPR-1/2, Pins, and LGN proteins (Kimple et al., 2002; Schaefer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kimple et al., 2002 and Schaefer et al., 2001.

claim: The preference of Gα for the GDP-bound state explains why RGS-7, a putative GAP, promotes spindle positioning.
source: This preference for the GDP-bound 'inactive' Gα state explains why RGS-7, a putative GTPase activating protein (GAP), promotes spindle positioning (Hess et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known biochemistry and supported by a citation.

claim: RIC-8 was shown to act as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) in vitro.
source: RIC-8 was shown to act as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) in vitro, while it may function in vivo as a Gα chaperone or as both a GEF and chaperone (Afshar et al., 2004; Afshar et al., 2005; David et al., 2005; Gabay et al., 2011; Hampoelz et al., 2005; Tall et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: RIC-8 may function in vivo as a Gα chaperone or as both a GEF and chaperone.
source: RIC-8 was shown to act as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) in vitro, while it may function in vivo as a Gα chaperone or as both a GEF and chaperone (Afshar et al., 2004; Afshar et al., 2005; David et al., 2005; Gabay et al., 2011; Hampoelz et al., 2005; Tall et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents uncertainty in the field.

claim: G-protein coupled receptors and Gαo∙GTP signaling contribute to spindle positioning in Drosophila neuroblasts and sensory organ precursor cells.
source: In addition to RIC-8, G-protein coupled receptors and Gαo∙GTP signaling contribute to spindle positioning in Drosophila neuroblasts and sensory organ precursor cells (Katanaev et al., 2005; Schaefer et al., 2001; Yoshiura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in Drosophila.

claim: It has been proposed that the Gα∙GTP-binding and hydrolysis cycle forms a critical step in cortical pulling force generation.
source: Therefore, it has been proposed that the Gα∙GTP-binding and hydrolysis cycle forms a critical step in cortical pulling force generation (Afshar et al., 2004; Srinivasan et al., 2003; Yoshiura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work, supported by citations.

claim: The C. elegans one-cell embryo undergoes reproducible spindle positioning and asymmetric cell division in the absence of cell-cell signaling.
source: We use the C. elegans one-cell embryo (P0), which undergoes reproducible spindle positioning and asymmetric cell division in the absence of cell-cell signaling (Video 1) (Rose and Gonczy, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and Video 1.

claim: Modifying endogenous genes with tunable light-controlled interacting protein tags (TULIPs) induced strong germline silencing.
source: As an initial hurdle, modifying endogenous genes with tunable light-controlled interacting protein tags (TULIPs) induced strong germline silencing.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experimental work.

claim: A new codon usage adaptation method (GLO, GermLine Optimized) was developed to promote expression of foreign sequences in the C. elegans germline.
source: We developed a strategy to promote expression of foreign sequences in the C. elegans germline, which is based in part on a new codon usage adaptation method (GLO, GermLine Optimized).
evidence: This describes a methodological development by the authors.

claim: Gα∙GDP and GPR-1/2 can be replaced with a light-inducible membrane anchor.
source: Our results show that Gα∙GDP and GPR-1/2 can be replaced with a light-inducible membrane anchor, while LIN-5 is required as activator of dynein-dependent cortical pulling force generation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LIN-5 is required as activator of dynein-dependent cortical pulling force generation.
source: Our results show that Gα∙GDP and GPR-1/2 can be replaced with a light-inducible membrane anchor, while LIN-5 is required as activator of dynein-dependent cortical pulling force generation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Local light-controlled LIN-5 recruitment enabled manipulation of spindle position and orientation.
source: Local light-controlled LIN-5 recruitment enabled us to manipulate the spindle position and orientation, and thereby the outcome of cell division in the early embryo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Local light-controlled LIN-5 recruitment enabled manipulation of the outcome of cell division in the early embryo.
source: Local light-controlled LIN-5 recruitment enabled us to manipulate the spindle position and orientation, and thereby the outcome of cell division in the early embryo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Cytoplasmic dynein and the Gα–GPR-1/2–LIN-5 complex overlap and function together in pulling force generation at the cell cortex of C. elegans early blastomeres.
source: Our previous studies and CRISPR/Cas9-assisted endogenous tagging demonstrated that cytoplasmic dynein and the Gα–GPR-1/2–LIN-5 complex overlap and function together in pulling force generation at the cell cortex of C. elegans early blastomeres (Figure 1b) (Portegijs et al., 2016; Schmidt et al., 2017; van der Voet et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and Figure 1b.

claim: Interfering with Gα, GPR-1/2, or LIN-5 function abolished significant force generation.
source: Interfering with Gα, GPR-1/2, or LIN-5 function abolished significant force generation, as previously reported (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and citations to previous work.

claim: RNA interference (RNAi) of ric-8 or rgs-7 by dsRNA injection resulted in partial loss of pulling forces.
source: RNA interference (RNAi) of ric-8 or rgs-7 by dsRNA injection resulted in partial loss of pulling forces (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Double ric-8(RNAi); rgs-7(RNAi) did not further decrease pulling forces.
source: Double ric-8(RNAi); rgs-7(RNAi) did not further decrease pulling forces as might be expected when RIC-8 and RGS-7 both promote a critical GTPase cycle (Hess et al., 2004; Srinivasan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: RNAi of ric-8 and rgs-7 is known to cause incomplete gene inactivation.
source: However, RNAi of ric-8 and rgs-7 is known to cause incomplete gene inactivation, which could also explain the limited defects.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about RNAi limitations.

claim: ric-8 and rgs-7 null mutants produce no or very few viable progeny.
source: To circumvent this caveat, we set out to generate germline-inducible knock-out alleles, as ric-8 and rgs-7 null mutants produce no or very few viable progeny (Hess et al., 2004; Reynolds et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ric-8lox knockout embryos showed reduced spindle pole peak velocities (anterior −50% and posterior −48%).
source: Compared to the control without CRE activity, knockout embryos showed reduced spindle pole peak velocities (ric-8lox: anterior −50% and posterior −48%; rgs-7lox: anterior −29% and posterior −11%), similar to or more defective than the corresponding RNAi embryos (Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: rgs-7lox knockout embryos showed reduced spindle pole peak velocities (anterior −29% and posterior −11%).
source: Compared to the control without CRE activity, knockout embryos showed reduced spindle pole peak velocities (ric-8lox: anterior −50% and posterior −48%; rgs-7lox: anterior −29% and posterior −11%), similar to or more defective than the corresponding RNAi embryos (Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The double knock-out of ric-8lox; rgs-7lox showed much reduced spindle pole movements (anterior −68% and posterior −67%), resembling Gα(RNAi).
source: Importantly, the double knock-out of ric-8lox; rgs-7lox showed much reduced spindle pole movements (anterior −68% and posterior −67%), thereby resembling Gα(RNAi) (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: RIC-8 and RGS-7 act independently, or partly redundant, as positive regulators of Gα.
source: This indicates that RIC-8 and RGS-7 act independently, or partly redundant, as positive regulators of Gα.
evidence: This is an inference from the double knockout data.

claim: A computational approach was developed to design protein-coding sequences resistant to silencing in the germline.
source: As introduction of epdz, lov, and cre sequences induced strong germline silencing responses, we developed a computational approach to design protein-coding sequences that are resistant to silencing in the germline.
evidence: This describes a methodological development by the authors.

claim: The design algorithm assembles a coding sequence for any desired polypeptide from a list of 12-nucleotide words found in native germline-expressed genes.
source: Our design algorithm assembles a coding sequence for any desired polypeptide from a list of 12-nucleotide words found in native germline-expressed genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the algorithm developed by the authors, illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transgenes designed using the germline optimization approach evade the germline silencing machinery.
source: We hypothesized that transgenes designed in this way would mimic native genes and thereby evade the germline silencing machinery. Indeed, using this approach, we could obtain robust expression of several foreign transgenes that were otherwise silenced (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most germline-optimized transgenes were stably expressed for many generations.
source: Although most of these transgenes were stably expressed for many generations, two out of 16 distinct constructs tested showed evidence of gradual silencing when passaging strains in culture (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: Two out of 16 distinct germline-optimized constructs showed evidence of gradual silencing when passaging strains in culture.
source: Although most of these transgenes were stably expressed for many generations, two out of 16 distinct constructs tested showed evidence of gradual silencing when passaging strains in culture (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: Combining germline-optimized exons with poly-AT-cluster rich intron sequences resulted in stable germline expression of eight out of eight transgenes.
source: Therefore, as a further buffer against silencing, we combined our germline-optimized exons with poly-AT-cluster rich intron sequences, which were recently demonstrated to protect against germline silencing (Frøkjær-Jensen et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018). This combined approach resulted in stable germline expression of eight out of eight transgenes and enabled implementation of the ePDZ–LOV system for use in the C. elegans early embryo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work on intron sequences.

claim: Poly-AT-cluster rich intron sequences protect against germline silencing.
source: Therefore, as a further buffer against silencing, we combined our germline-optimized exons with poly-AT-cluster rich intron sequences, which were recently demonstrated to protect against germline silencing (Frøkjær-Jensen et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Illumination with a blue (491 nm) laser rapidly induced recruitment of ePDZ::mCherry to PH::LOV.
source: Illumination with a blue (491 nm) laser rapidly induced recruitment of ePDZ::mCherry to PH::LOV, and allowed both global and local cortical enrichment in one-cell embryos (Figure 2b and Videos 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and Videos 3–5.

claim: The ePDZ–LOV system allowed both global and local cortical enrichment in one-cell embryos.
source: Illumination with a blue (491 nm) laser rapidly induced recruitment of ePDZ::mCherry to PH::LOV, and allowed both global and local cortical enrichment in one-cell embryos (Figure 2b and Videos 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and Videos 3–5.

claim: The dissociation kinetics of ePDZ::mCherry from the membrane after a global activation pulse had a half-time of 42 seconds.
source: To test the reversibility of the ePDZ–LOV interaction, we followed ePDZ::mCherry membrane localization after a global activation pulse, and found dissociation kinetics similar to those reported by others (Hallett et al., 2016) (t½=42 s; Figure 2c and Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c and Video 6.

claim: The ePDZ–LOV system is suitable for controlled protein localization in the early C. elegans embryo.
source: Thus, we conclude that the ePDZ–LOV system is suitable for controlled protein localization in the early C. elegans embryo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the characterization experiments.

claim: Global cortical enrichment of RGS-7 enhanced spindle pole movements (anterior +25% and posterior +20%).
source: Global cortical enrichment of RGS-7 enhanced spindle pole movements (anterior +25% and posterior +20%) (Figure 3b) and spindle oscillations (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: Global cortical enrichment of RGS-7 enhanced spindle oscillations.
source: Global cortical enrichment of RGS-7 enhanced spindle pole movements (anterior +25% and posterior +20%) (Figure 3b) and spindle oscillations (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Recruitment of RGS-7::ePDZ to PAR-6::LOV enhanced the peak velocities of both spindle poles, most significantly the anterior pole (anterior +25% and posterior +14%).
source: Following global light exposure, recruitment of RGS-7::ePDZ to PAR-6::LOV enhanced the peak velocities of both spindle poles, but most significantly the movement of the anterior pole (anterior +25% and posterior +14%; Figure 3b,c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: Cortical recruitment of RGS-7 acutely increases pulling forces, in agreement with its proposed function as a GAP that promotes Gα∙GDP–GPR-1/2 interaction.
source: Thus, cortical recruitment of RGS-7 acutely increases pulling forces, in agreement with its proposed function as a GAP that promotes Gα∙GDP–GPR-1/2 interaction.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data combined with known biochemistry.

claim: Cortical enrichment of RIC-8 did not significantly enhance pulling forces.
source: In contrast, cortical enrichment of RIC-8 did not significantly enhance pulling forces (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The ric-8lox; rgs-7lox synergistic phenotype supports a model in which RIC-8 and RGS-7 promote Gα function at different levels.
source: Thus, in agreement with the ric-8lox; rgs-7lox synergistic phenotype, our optogenetic localization experiments support a model in which RIC-8 and RGS-7 promote Gα function at different levels.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined knockout and optogenetic data.

claim: RGS-7 probably functions as a GAP.
source: While RGS-7 probably functions as a GAP, our data are in line with RIC-8 acting in vivo as a Gα chaperone, rather than a GEF, thus indirectly promoting force generation.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The data are in line with RIC-8 acting in vivo as a Gα chaperone, rather than a GEF.
source: While RGS-7 probably functions as a GAP, our data are in line with RIC-8 acting in vivo as a Gα chaperone, rather than a GEF, thus indirectly promoting force generation.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Gα∙GTP has been reported to affect spindle orientation in specific tissues.
source: Despite the observed replaceability of Gα with a general membrane anchor, Gα∙GTP has been reported to affect the spindle orientation in specific tissues (Katanaev et al., 2005; Schaefer et al., 2001; Yoshiura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In Drosophila neuroblasts and sensory organ precursor cells, canonical G-protein signaling is used to align cellular polarity with tissue polarity.
source: In Drosophila neuroblasts and sensory organ precursor cells, canonical G-protein signaling is used to align cellular polarity with tissue polarity (Katanaev et al., 2005; Yoshiura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Gα∙GTP may indirectly contribute to spindle positioning.
source: As such, Gα∙GTP may indirectly contribute to spindle positioning.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cited work.

claim: One of the Drosophila Pins GoLoco domains was found to preferentially interact with Gαo∙GTP.
source: In addition, one of the Drosophila Pins GoLoco domains was found to preferentially interact with Gαo∙GTP, thereby linking the spindle positioning machinery with canonical G-protein signaling (Kopein and Katanaev, 2009; Yoshiura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Light-induced ePDZ::GPR-1 recruitment increased spindle pole movements (anterior +56% and posterior +10%).
source: However, light-induced ePDZ::GPR-1 recruitment increased spindle pole movements (anterior +56% and posterior +10%) (Figure 5d, f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d and 5f.

claim: Membrane-localized ePDZ::GPR-1 sustained force generation in the absence of Gα (anterior +195% and posterior +232%).
source: Moreover, membrane-localized ePDZ::GPR-1 sustained force generation in the absence of Gα (anterior +195% and posterior +232%), indicating that Gα is dispensable for cortical pulling force generation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Gα is dispensable for cortical pulling force generation.
source: Moreover, membrane-localized ePDZ::GPR-1 sustained force generation in the absence of Gα (anterior +195% and posterior +232%), indicating that Gα is dispensable for cortical pulling force generation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Recruitment of ePDZ::GPR-1 restored spindle pole movements to a similar degree in Gα(RNAi) and Gα(RNAi); ric-8(RNAi) embryos.
source: Recruitment of ePDZ::GPR-1 restored spindle pole movements to a similar degree in Gα(RNAi) and Gα(RNAi); ric-8(RNAi) embryos (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Cortical pulling forces can be generated when the Gα membrane anchor function is replaced by PH::LOV, most likely in the absence of Gαi/o∙GTP.
source: Thus, cortical pulling forces can be generated when the Gα membrane anchor function is replaced by PH::LOV, and most likely in the absence of Gαi/o∙GTP.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Gα functions as a membrane anchor.
source: We conclude that Gα functions as a membrane anchor and that Gα∙GTP does not perform an essential function in pulling force generation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Gα∙GTP does not perform an essential function in pulling force generation.
source: We conclude that Gα functions as a membrane anchor and that Gα∙GTP does not perform an essential function in pulling force generation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The presence of blue light resulted in substantially elevated spindle pulling forces when compared to dark state experiments (anterior +33% and posterior +35%).
source: Nevertheless, the presence of blue light resulted in substantially elevated spindle pulling forces when compared to dark state experiments (anterior +33% and posterior +35%) (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The observed spindle pole movements are light-dependent and the specific result of inducible cortical recruitment of GPR-1.
source: We conclude that the observed spindle pole movements are light-dependent and the specific result of inducible cortical recruitment of GPR-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the dark state control experiments.

claim: Cortical pulling events cause inward movements of the plasma membrane, visible as extended invaginations.
source: Cortical pulling events cause inward movements of the plasma membrane, which are visible by spinning disk-confocal fluorescence microscopy as extended invaginations of the plasma membrane (Redemann et al., 2010) (Figure 5g and Videos 10 and 11).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and experimental data shown in Figure 5g and Videos 10 and 11.

claim: Membrane invaginations occur in wild type embryos, depend on microtubules and cortical force generator components, and correlate with the distribution of pulling force generators.
source: These membrane invaginations occur in wild type embryos, depend on microtubules and cortical force generator components, and correlate with the distribution of pulling force generators (Redemann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Membrane invaginations most likely reveal the presence and distribution of active individual force generators.
source: Therefore, these membrane invaginations most likely reveal the presence and distribution of active individual force generators.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited work and the authors' observations.

claim: Control PH::GFP embryos showed on average 138 membrane invaginations during anaphase in an area covering approximately 1/3 of the cell surface.
source: Control PH::GFP embryos showed on average 138 membrane invaginations during anaphase in an area covering approximately 1/3 of the cell surface (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The distribution of membrane invaginations reflected the three described cortical domains: anterior, posterior, and a posterior lateral region at ±60% embryo length.
source: When plotted along the anterior-posterior axis, the distribution of these invaginations reflected the three described cortical domains: anterior, posterior, and a posterior lateral region at ±60% embryo length (Rose and Gonczy, 2014) (Figure 5h-left).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5h and a citation.

claim: The posterior lateral band region localizes the LET-99 DEP-domain protein, which antagonizes the localization of GPR-1/2 and thereby pulling force generation.
source: The posterior lateral band region localizes the LET-99 DEP-domain protein, which antagonizes the localization of GPR-1/2 and thereby pulling force generation (Krueger et al., 2010; Tsou et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: LET-99 explains the absence of invaginations around 60% embryo length.
source: This explains the absence of invaginations around 60% embryo length (Figure 5h-left).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of LET-99 and the observed distribution.

claim: Cortical GPR-1 recruitment resulted in a total number of 174 (+25% compared to ph::lov control) invaginations in the presence of Gα.
source: Cortical GPR-1 recruitment resulted in a total number of 174 (+25% compared to ph::lov control) invaginations in the presence, and 122 invaginations (+249% compared to Gα(RNAi) embryos) in the absence of Gα (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cortical GPR-1 recruitment resulted in 122 invaginations (+249% compared to Gα(RNAi) embryos) in the absence of Gα.
source: Cortical GPR-1 recruitment resulted in a total number of 174 (+25% compared to ph::lov control) invaginations in the presence, and 122 invaginations (+249% compared to Gα(RNAi) embryos) in the absence of Gα (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: GPR-1 recruitment to the membrane induces cortical pulling forces, even in the apparent absence of Gα proteins.
source: Thus, in agreement with our observations in spindle severing assays, GPR-1 recruitment to the membrane induces cortical pulling forces, even in the apparent absence of Gα proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the invagination counting data.

claim: The lack of invaginations around 60% embryo length was no longer detected when ePDZ::GPR-1 was recruited to PH::LOV.
source: The lack of invaginations around 60% embryo length was no longer detected when ePDZ::GPR-1 was recruited to PH::LOV.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The characteristic dip in cortical GPR-1 localization was no longer detected after ectopic GPR-1 recruitment.
source: In agreement, the characteristic dip in cortical GPR-1 localization (e.g.: Figure 1b) was no longer detected after ectopic GPR-1 recruitment (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of Figure 1b and Figure 5b.

claim: LET-99 does not antagonize the cortical recruitment of ePDZ::GPR-1 by PH::LOV, in contrast to the Gα∙GDP-mediated localization of endogenous GPR-1/2.
source: Thus, as expected, LET-99 does not antagonize the cortical recruitment of ePDZ::GPR-1 by PH::LOV, in contrast to the Gα∙GDP-mediated localization of endogenous GPR-1/2.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed distribution of invaginations.

claim: The remaining peak numbers of invaginations likely represent the cortical regions closest to the spindle poles.
source: The remaining peak numbers of invaginations likely represent the cortical regions closest to the spindle poles, as these sites contact the highest numbers of astral microtubules.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known biology of spindle-cortex interactions.

claim: Gα is not essential for force generation.
source: Taken together, Gα is not essential for force generation, but the characteristic distribution of force generating events is likely regulated in part at the Gα protein or Gα–GPR-1/2 protein interaction level.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The characteristic distribution of force generating events is likely regulated in part at the Gα protein or Gα–GPR-1/2 protein interaction level.
source: Taken together, Gα is not essential for force generation, but the characteristic distribution of force generating events is likely regulated in part at the Gα protein or Gα–GPR-1/2 protein interaction level.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed distribution patterns.

claim: The Gα–GPR-1/2–LIN-5 complex has been suggested to function as a dynein anchor.
source: The Gα–GPR-1/2–LIN-5 complex has been suggested to function as a dynein anchor (Kotak et al., 2012; di Pietro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Induced ePDZ::DHC-1 cortical recruitment in the presence of the wild type complex slightly increased spindle pole movements (anterior +10% and posterior +5%, 162 membrane invaginations:+17%).
source: We found that induced ePDZ::DHC-1 cortical recruitment in the presence of the wild type complex slightly (but not significantly) increased spindle pole movements (anterior +10% and posterior +5%, 162 membrane invaginations:+17%; Figure 6d–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d-f.

claim: Cortical ePDZ::DHC-1 recruitment in the absence of a wild type complex did not result in substantial pulling force generation, spindle movements, or membrane invaginations.
source: Notably, however, cortical ePDZ::DHC-1 recruitment in the absence of a wild type complex (Gα(RNAi), gpr-1/2(RNAi) or lin-5(RNAi) embryos) did not result in substantial pulling force generation, spindle movements, or membrane invaginations (Figure 6d–f and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d-f and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Direct cortical dynein anchoring does not support force generation.
source: Because direct cortical dynein anchoring does not support force generation, it is likely that the LIN-5 complex performs essential functions beyond providing a structural dynein anchor.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the dynein recruitment experiments.

claim: The LIN-5 complex likely performs essential functions beyond providing a structural dynein anchor.
source: Because direct cortical dynein anchoring does not support force generation, it is likely that the LIN-5 complex performs essential functions beyond providing a structural dynein anchor.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Cortical LIN-5 recruitment greatly increased spindle pulling forces in otherwise wild type embryos (anterior +131% and posterior +68%, 557 invaginations:+303%).
source: Spindle severing experiments and invagination counting revealed that cortical LIN-5 recruitment greatly increased spindle pulling forces in otherwise wild type embryos (anterior +131% and posterior +68%, 557 invaginations:+303%) (Figure 7d,e and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d, 7e, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: gpr-1/2(RNAi) embryos showed strong dynein-dependent forces after cortical recruitment of LIN-5 (anterior +183% and posterior +244%, 429 invaginations:+1488%).
source: gpr-1/2(RNAi) embryos also showed strong dynein-dependent forces after cortical recruitment of LIN-5 (anterior +183% and posterior +244%, 429 invaginations:+1488%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Cortical LIN-5 recruitment generated extreme premature pulling forces that could result in separation of centrosomes and their associated pronuclei even before formation of a bipolar spindle.
source: In fact, cortical LIN-5 recruitment generated extreme premature pulling forces (Video 16) that could result in separation of centrosomes and their associated pronuclei even before formation of a bipolar spindle (Video 17).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Videos 16 and 17.

claim: LIN-5 is a strong activator of dynein in the generation of cortical pulling forces.
source: These results identify LIN-5 as a strong activator of dynein in the generation of cortical pulling forces.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the LIN-5 recruitment experiments.

claim: Similarly high pulling forces were observed upon cortical LIN-5 recruitment in gpr-1/2(RNAi) and Gα(RNAi) embryos.
source: We observed similarly high pulling forces upon cortical LIN-5 recruitment in gpr-1/2(RNAi) and Gα(RNAi) embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither Gα nor GPR-1/2 are required for force generation.
source: Thus, neither Gα nor GPR-1/2 are required for force generation, and this particular context did not reveal a positive contribution of Gα∙GTP either.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the LIN-5 recruitment experiments in different genetic backgrounds.

claim: Cortical recruitment of LIN-5 localized dynein to the cortex.
source: In immunofluorescence staining experiments, we observed that cortical recruitment of LIN-5 localized dynein to the cortex (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: LIN-5 was detected at the cortex following the direct recruitment of ePDZ::DHC-1 to PH::LOV, even after knockdown of gpr-1/2 by RNAi.
source: Notably, the reverse was also seen: we detected LIN-5 at the cortex following the direct recruitment of ePDZ::DHC-1 to PH::LOV, even after knockdown of gpr-1/2 by RNAi (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, top).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The p150(Glued) dynactin subunit DNC-1 was present at the cell cortex when dynein was recruited to PH::LOV.
source: The p150(Glued) dynactin subunit DNC-1 was also present at the cell cortex of such embryos, which indicates that at least some PH::LOV-localized dynein complexes contain the dynactin cofactor (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, lower panels).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: DNC-1p150 colocalized with PH::LOV membrane-recruited dynein even in lin-5(RNAi) embryos.
source: DNC-1p150 colocalized with PH::LOV membrane-recruited dynein even in lin-5(RNAi) embryos.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: The cortical localization of dynein through a direct PH::LOV interaction leads to co-recruitment of LIN-5 and dynactin, but not to significant force generation.
source: Thus, the cortical localization of dynein through a direct PH::LOV interaction leads to co-recruitment of LIN-5 and dynactin, but not to significant force generation.
evidence: This is a summary of the observations from the dynein recruitment experiments.

claim: It is possible that dynein complexes recruited directly to the cortex adapt an inactive conformation or lack specific subunits of the dynein-dynactin motor complex.
source: It is possible that these complexes adapt an inactive conformation or lack specific subunits of the dynein-dynactin motor complex.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the lack of force generation.

claim: Dynein anchored at the cell cortex through the LIN-5 intermediate generated strong pulling forces.
source: In contrast, dynein anchored at the cell cortex through the LIN-5 intermediate generated strong pulling forces.
evidence: This is a summary of the LIN-5 recruitment results.

claim: Association with membrane-attached LIN-5 is essential for dynein to generate cortical pulling forces.
source: Together, these data indicate that association with membrane-attached LIN-5 is essential for dynein to generate cortical pulling forces.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined dynein and LIN-5 recruitment experiments.

claim: Local recruitment of LIN-5 to the anterior cortex from metaphase onwards caused the P0 spindle to position anteriorly, which inverted the AB:P1 size asymmetry after cell division.
source: Local recruitment of LIN-5 to the anterior cortex from metaphase onwards caused the P0 spindle to position anteriorly, which inverted the AB:P1 size asymmetry after cell division (Figure 8a and Video 18).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8a and Video 18.

claim: Recruiting LIN-5 laterally induced a completely perpendicular spindle position.
source: In addition, recruiting LIN-5 laterally induced a completely perpendicular spindle position (Figure 8b and Video 19).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8b and Video 19.

claim: In two-cell gpr-1/2(RNAi) embryos, the spindle fails to rotate in P1, resulting in a transverse spindle orientation in both blastomeres.
source: In two-cell gpr-1/2(RNAi) embryos, the spindle fails to rotate in P1, resulting in a transverse spindle orientation in both blastomeres (Srinivasan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Local recruitment of LIN-5 to the membranes between AB and P1 promoted anterior-posterior spindle orientations in both blastomeres of gpr-1/2(RNAi) embryos.
source: Importantly, local recruitment of LIN-5 to the membranes between AB and P1 promoted anterior-posterior spindle orientations in both blastomeres of gpr-1/2(RNAi) embryos (Figure 8c and Videos 20 and 21).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8c and Videos 20 and 21.

claim: Spindles maintained their anterior-posterior orientation throughout mitosis and induced cleavage furrows that reproducibly followed the spindle position.
source: These spindles maintained their anterior-posterior orientation throughout mitosis and induced cleavage furrows that reproducibly followed the spindle position.
evidence: This is an observation from the local LIN-5 recruitment experiments.

claim: These experiments underline the determining role of LIN-5-dependent cortical pulling in spindle orientation and cell cleavage plane determination.
source: These experiments underline the determining role of LIN-5-dependent cortical pulling in spindle orientation and cell cleavage plane determination.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the local manipulation experiments.

claim: Observations in two different systems indicate that dynein activation at microtubule plus ends requires the LIN-5/NuMA adaptor protein.
source: Thus, observations in two different systems indicate that dynein activation at microtubule plus ends requires the LIN-5/NuMA adaptor protein, similar to the requirement for an activating dynein adaptor in cargo transport (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current study with a recent study in human cells, supported by citations.

claim: Activation by LIN-5NuMA specifically promotes dynein function in generating membrane associated pulling forces.
source: It is tempting to speculate that activation by LIN-5NuMA specifically promotes dynein function in generating membrane associated pulling forces.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: In the cytoplasm, dynein adopts an inactive conformation and does not show processive movement in the absence of an activating adaptor.
source: In the cytoplasm, dynein adopts an inactive conformation and does not show processive movement in the absence of an activating adaptor (Reck-Peterson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Adaptor proteins such as BicD2 and Hook3 interact with specific cargo as well as with the dynein tail regions and the universal activating complex dynactin.
source: Adaptor proteins such as BicD2 and Hook3 interact with specific cargo as well as with the dynein tail regions and the universal activating complex dynactin (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Adaptor proteins promote the formation of stable and active dynein–dynactin-adaptor complexes.
source: Thereby, these adaptors promote the formation of stable and active dynein–dynactin-adaptor complexes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from cited work.

claim: The coiled-coil regions of the adaptors extend in between dynein and dynactin, with multiple adaptor-specific interaction sites.
source: Recent stuctural analyses revealed that the coiled-coil regions of the adaptors extend in between dynein and dynactin, with multiple adaptor-specific interaction sites, and with several adaptors promoting the recruitment of two dynein complexes in parallel (Grotjahn et al., 2018; Sladewski et al., 2018; Urnavicius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claim: Several adaptors promote the recruitment of two dynein complexes in parallel.
source: Recent stuctural analyses revealed that the coiled-coil regions of the adaptors extend in between dynein and dynactin, with multiple adaptor-specific interaction sites, and with several adaptors promoting the recruitment of two dynein complexes in parallel (Grotjahn et al., 2018; Sladewski et al., 2018; Urnavicius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claim: It is likely that dynein-dependent cortical pulling forces also involve an activating adaptor.
source: Although structural studies have focused on factors promoting minus-end directed transport, it is likely that dynein-dependent cortical pulling forces also involve an activating adaptor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known requirements for dynein activation.

claim: LIN-5NuMA could promote the assembly of stable dynein–dynactin complexes and release dynein autoinhibition.
source: As such, LIN-5NuMA could promote the assembly of stable dynein–dynactin complexes and release dynein autoinhibition.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known functions of other adaptors.

claim: The lack of pulling forces despite co-recruitment of LIN-5NuMA and DNC-1p150 together with dynein may indicate that the complex needs to be anchored through LIN-5 to achieve a specific conformation.
source: The lack of pulling forces, despite co-recruitment of LIN-5NuMA and DNC-1p150 together with dynein, may indicate that the complex needs to be anchored through LIN-5 in order to achieve a specific conformation and facilitate microtubule end-on pulling forces.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the experimental observations.

claim: A requirement for anchoring through LIN-5 could prevent inappropriate activation of dynein–dynactin–LIN-5NuMA complexes in the cytoplasm.
source: Such a requirement could prevent inappropriate activation of dynein–dynactin–LIN-5NuMA complexes in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential regulatory mechanism.

claim: In the optogenetic experiments in human carcinoma cells, dynein localized p150 at the membrane, but NuMA was not observed to be co-recruited.
source: In the optogenetic experiments in human carcinoma cells, dynein also localized p150 at the membrane, however in contrast to our findings, NuMA was not observed to be co-recruited in this study (Okumura et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from another study, supported by a citation.

claim: The discrepancy in NuMA co-recruitment might be related to the remarkably different kinetics of the two systems.
source: While the reason for this discrepancy is currently unknown, it might be related to the remarkably different kinetics of the two systems.
evidence: This is speculation to explain differences between studies.

claim: Using the TULIP system, membrane localization of ePDZ-tagged endogenous proteins was observed within seconds.
source: Using the TULIP system, we observed membrane localization of ePDZ-tagged endogenous proteins within seconds, whereas in the iLID experiments in human carcinoma cells accumulation took place over multiple minutes.
evidence: This is a comparison of the kinetics in the two systems.

claim: In the iLID experiments in human carcinoma cells, accumulation took place over multiple minutes.
source: Using the TULIP system, we observed membrane localization of ePDZ-tagged endogenous proteins within seconds, whereas in the iLID experiments in human carcinoma cells accumulation took place over multiple minutes.
evidence: This is a comparison with another study.

claim: It is possible that in the longer time frame, cytoplasmic dynein complexes are recruited to the cortex with adaptors other than NuMA.
source: It is possible that in the longer time frame, cytoplasmic dynein complexes are recruited to the cortex with adaptors other than NuMA.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the differences between systems.

claim: In yeast, dynein is localized by the single-component cortical anchor Num1, a coiled-coil domain protein with a PH-domain for membrane localization.
source: In yeast, dynein is localized by the single-component cortical anchor Num1, a coiled-coil domain protein with a PH-domain for membrane localization (Ananthanarayanan, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Membrane-tethered LIN-5 could suffice as a dynein anchor and activator.
source: Our ectopic ePDZ–LOV heterodimerization experiments show that membrane-tethered LIN-5 could suffice as a dynein anchor and activator, and that local regulation is needed to rotate and displace the spindle.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Local regulation is needed to rotate and displace the spindle.
source: Our ectopic ePDZ–LOV heterodimerization experiments show that membrane-tethered LIN-5 could suffice as a dynein anchor and activator, and that local regulation is needed to rotate and displace the spindle.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The trimeric dynein anchor/adaptor evolved in metazoans to augment context-specific regulation and reduce stochastic activation of spindle pulling forces.
source: Conceivably, the trimeric dynein anchor/adaptor evolved in metazoans to augment context-specific regulation and reduce stochastic activation of spindle pulling forces.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary advantage of the complex.

claim: The LET-99 protein was previously reported to restrict the localization of GPR-1/2 in a posterior-lateral band region of the one-cell embryo.
source: The LET-99 protein was previously reported to restrict the localization of GPR-1/2 in a posterior-lateral band region of the one-cell embryo, thereby contributing to higher net pulling forces in the posterior direction (Tsou et al., 2002; Tsou et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Direct membrane recruitment of GPR-1 overcomes LET-99 regulation, in agreement with LET-99 normally antagonizing Gα∙GDP–GPR-1/2 interaction.
source: Our observation that direct membrane recruitment of GPR-1 overcomes this regulation is in agreement with LET-99 normally antagonizing Gα∙GDP–GPR-1/2 interaction.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The ric-8 gene was discovered through 'resistant to inhibitors of cholinesterase 8' mutants in C. elegans, which are defective in Gαq-stimulated neurotransmitter release.
source: The ric-8 gene was discovered through 'resistant to inhibitors of cholinesterase 8' mutants in C. elegans, which are defective in Gαq-stimulated neurotransmitter release (Miller et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original discovery.

claim: The discovery that ric-8 acts also with GOA-1 in spindle positioning indicated a general role for RIC-8 in Gα regulation.
source: The discovery that ric-8 acts also with GOA-1 in spindle positioning indicated a general role for RIC-8 in Gα regulation (Miller and Rand, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Mammalian RIC-8A acts as a non-receptor GEF, which does not activate Gαβγ trimers, but shows higher affinity for free Gα∙GDP and the Gα∙GDP–LGN–NuMA complex.
source: Based on in vitro experiments, mammalian RIC-8A acts as a non-receptor GEF, which surprisingly does not activate Gαβγ trimers, but shows higher affinity for free Gα∙GDP and the Gα∙GDP–LGN–NuMA complex (Tall and Gilman, 2005; Tall et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: Experiments in Drosophila and mouse embryonic stem cells demonstrated a chaperone function of RIC-8 required for the cortical localization of Gα subunits.
source: In contrast, experiments in Drosophila and mouse embryonic stem cells demonstrated a chaperone function required for the cortical localization of Gα subunits (David et al., 2005; Gabay et al., 2011; Hampoelz et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in Drosophila and mouse.

claim: Only the Drosophila Gαi protein forms a complex with Pins–Mud.
source: Only the Drosophila Gαi protein forms a complex with Pins–Mud (Schaefer et al., 2001), and Drosophila Gαi, but not Gαo, depends on RIC-8 for its cortical localization (David et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in Drosophila.

claim: Drosophila Gαi, but not Gαo, depends on RIC-8 for its cortical localization.
source: Only the Drosophila Gαi protein forms a complex with Pins–Mud (Schaefer et al., 2001), and Drosophila Gαi, but not Gαo, depends on RIC-8 for its cortical localization (David et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study in Drosophila.

claim: C. elegans RIC-8 was shown to exhibit both GEF and chaperone activity, depending on the Gα subunit.
source: Seemingly unifying these independently described RIC-8 functions, C. elegans RIC-8 was shown to exhibit both GEF and chaperone activity, depending on the Gα subunit (Afshar et al., 2004; Afshar et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in C. elegans.

claim: The C. elegans GOA-1 and GPA-16 Gα proteins act in a substantially redundant manner in spindle positioning.
source: The C. elegans GOA-1 and GPA-16 Gα proteins act in a substantially redundant manner in spindle positioning, but diverge in other ways.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: GPA-16 is closest to the Gαi class, has been implicated only in spindle positioning, and depends on RIC-8 for its cortical localization.
source: GPA-16 is closest to the Gαi class, has been implicated only in spindle positioning, and depends on RIC-8 for its cortical localization (Afshar et al., 2005; Bergmann et al., 2003; Gotta and Ahringer, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both C. elegans and Drosophila RIC-8 appears to act as a chaperone for Gαi to promote spindle positioning.
source: Thus, both C. elegans and Drosophila RIC-8 appears to act as a chaperone for Gαi to promote spindle positioning.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of C. elegans and Drosophila data.

claim: The Gαo GOA-1 subunit does not require RIC-8 for its membrane localization.
source: Also similar to Drosophila, the Gαo GOA-1 subunit does not require RIC-8 for its membrane localization (David et al., 2005; Afshar et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RIC-8 was reported to act as a GEF for GOA-1.
source: Instead, RIC-8 was reported to act as a GEF for GOA-1 (Afshar et al., 2004), and is usually considered to act as a GEF for Gαq and Gαo in neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RIC-8 is usually considered to act as a GEF for Gαq and Gαo in neurotransmitter release.
source: Instead, RIC-8 was reported to act as a GEF for GOA-1 (Afshar et al., 2004), and is usually considered to act as a GEF for Gαq and Gαo in neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The contribution of a Gαo GEF in spindle positioning would mean that either Gα∙GTP or Gα∙GDP/GTP cycling promotes spindle pulling forces.
source: However, the contribution of a Gαo GEF in spindle positioning would mean that either Gα∙GTP or Gα∙GDP/GTP cycling promotes spindle pulling forces.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what a GEF function would imply.

claim: Both possibilities (Gα∙GTP or Gα∙GDP/GTP cycling promoting forces) seem unlikely in light of the results described.
source: Both of these possibilities seem unlikely in light of the results described here.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The fact that Gα can be replaced with a PH–membrane anchor dismisses a general requirement for Gα∙GTP in pulling force generation.
source: The fact that Gα can be replaced with a PH–membrane anchor dismisses a general requirement for Gα∙GTP in pulling force generation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: RIC-8 functioning in a Gα∙GDP/GTP cycle is not supported by the knockout and membrane localization studies.
source: Moreover, RIC-8 functioning in a Gα∙GDP/GTP cycle is not supported by our knockout and membrane localization studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: There is reason to question whether RIC-8 really functions as a GEF.
source: Therefore, there is reason to question whether RIC-8 really functions as a GEF.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The strongest support for RIC-8 functioning as a GEF has come from in vitro experiments, in which RIC-8 showed rather inefficient GEF activity towards Gα∙GDP.
source: The strongest support for such a function has come from in vitro experiments, in which RIC-8 showed rather inefficient GEF activity towards Gα∙GDP (Kant et al., 2016; Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: It appears conceivable that incubation of Gα with a chaperone that affects its folding causes nucleotide dissociation.
source: It appears conceivable that incubation of Gα with a chaperone that affects its folding causes nucleotide dissociation.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the in vitro GEF activity.

claim: If correct, the membrane localized GOA-1 in ric-8 mutants would reflect an incompletely functional form.
source: If correct, the membrane localized GOA-1 in ric-8 mutants would reflect an incompletely functional form.
evidence: This is speculation about the nature of GOA-1 in ric-8 mutants.
